title: Dose-Dependent Febrile Response to Transcranial Pulse Stimulation Reveals Reversible Iatrogenic Calcification Misattributed to Multiple Sclerosis Progression
content: Background/Objectives: In multiple sclerosis (MS), deterioration occurring independently of new focal inflammatory activity may be attributed to disease progression, and treatment escalated on that basis. This case report describes a patient in whom that attribution misdirected treatment for nearly six years, and how a patient-initiated investigation—triggered by an anomalous dose-dependent response to transcranial pulse stimulation (TPS)—revealed a reversible, iatrogenic mechanism underlying the decline. Case Presentation: A 51-year-old male with relapsing-remitting MS and undiagnosed genetic polymorphisms (VDR Bsm1 +/+; CACNA1C +/+; CBS/MTRR transsulfuration variants) underwent a high-dose vitamin D protocol (80,000 IU/day) for five years and eight months, despite an already-optimal baseline 25-hydroxyvitamin D and mineral dysregulation (hypercalciuria, hyperphosphaturia, hypercortisolism) documented eight years earlier. The protocol's premise—that the patient was vitamin D resistant—was undercut by his own data: this was supraphysiological dosing layered onto a pre-existing mineral-handling disorder. The subsequent decline—acrocyanosis, nephrocalcinosis, scoliosis, tissue necrosis, and wheelchair dependence—was attributed to MS progression and met with escalating interventions rather than investigation of the underlying metabolic driver. Throughout, the kidney functioned as the sentinel organ: renal pathology was documented from adolescence, biochemically demonstrable nearly a decade before the protocol, and progressed to radiographic capsular linear calcification during treatment. The decisive diagnostic signal was a reproducible, dose-dependent acute response to transcranial pulse stimulation, characterized by chills within 1–2 hours progressing to fever with rigors. Methods: Genetic profiling across six metabolic systems (including vitamin D clearance, vitamin K cycle, magnesium, calcium signaling, detoxification, and immune regulation) via two independent direct-to-consumer platforms, longitudinal organic acids testing, serial mineral/hormonal panels, and toxic metal provocation (DMPS) were undertaken. Results: Metabolic profiling confirmed progressive mitochondrial dysfunction and transsulfuration collapse during high-dose vitamin D; DMPS provocation documented a residual mercury burden (96 μg/g creatinine; reference < 0.8) despite years of chelation—a finding consistent with sequestration of mercury within ectopic calcium-phosphate deposits. Following vitamin D cessation and metabolic correction (vitamin K2, magnesium, mitochondrial support), the patient improved substantially within six weeks—from wheelchair dependence to independent swimming (500 m) and 30 m assisted walking—with near resolution of scoliosis and healing of necrotic tissue. Conclusions: This patient's decline was consistent with a reversible, iatrogenic calcium-phosphate dysregulation driven by high-dose vitamin D in a genetically susceptible host. A multi-hit genomic architecture—spanning impaired vitamin D clearance (CYP24A1/VDR), impaired vitamin K-dependent calcification inhibition (VKORC1/GGCX/CYP4F2), magnesium wasting (TRPM6/CNNM2/SLC41A1), calcium channel variants (CACNA1C/TRPM3), and detoxification failure (GSTM1 Null)—is offered as one hypothesis to explain why this outcome occurred in this patient. The variant calls derive from two independent direct-to-consumer genotyping platforms and require clinical-grade confirmation before they can support established mechanistic claims. If confirmed, this architecture would render the outcome biochemically predictable - the foreseeable consequence of supraphysiological vitamin D dosing in a genetically susceptible host - rather than idiosyncratic. The case illustrates how a symptom-based diagnostic label can misdirect treatment while the treatable mechanistic driver goes unaddressed and argues for interrogation of the kidney's mineral-handling status before any high-dose vitamin D or neuromodulatory intervention. We hypothesize—on the basis of the dose-dependent, febrile responses to TPS, and given TPS's shockwave lineage originally engineered to fragment calcific deposits—that TPS dose-sensitivity may serve as a diagnostic tool to identify patients whose deterioration is driven by metabolic-perfusion failure rather than by the condition named in their diagnosis, and that a subset of demyelinating lesions may harbor a calcium-phosphate component warranting prospective investigation. These are offered as hypotheses requiring validation, not established conclusions.
